title: Astrological and medical compilation with occasional words written in cipher

Probably the common vowel-substitution of English medical manuscripts (cf. HU 1051, where the cataloguer read 'Pr4pt2r 1m4r2m m5l32r3s'). Fully digitised on HDL. Not in the repo. First pass 28 Oct 2026 (targets/hm64/): ff. 163r and 111r viewed on HDL; the red hatched boxes on 163r/163v are crosses in Latin charms, not cipher; two candidate cipher words located (163r heading 'T R y 6 z l e t h', 111r heading 'S C G e G N T'), neither read; ff. 50r and 143r show none; f. 102v and the versos unviewed. Vowel-to-number substitution not confirmed.

title: Philip IV to Juan de Velasco y la Cueva, conde de Siruela, ambassador in Genoa: despatch entirely in cipher (PARES title "Minuta de despacho cifrada")
folio_note: 4 images online; 3⅓ pages, entirely in cipher except the address; signed "Yo el Rey"
status: Swept 28 Oct 2026 (Brice Dudout's PARES sweep, facet filter idFI); "cifrada", 17th century: "Minuta de despacho cifrada a Juan de Velasco y la Cueva, conde de Siruela". Images viewed: 3 pages of symbol cipher with short clear passages, signed "Yo el Rey"; no decipherment visible. Sibling of the Genoa 1638-51 row already in the catalogue (Velasco y la Cueva, Eraso…), which may give the key family. Corrected 28 Oct 2026 after a full transcription (64 lines, 1,818 tokens): not a minute with clear passages but a despatch entirely in cipher (only the address in clear), dated 20 Nov 1638, in the Genoa 1638 system (genes1638 key family) with extra chancery signs (ℰ, ꝓ, ʒ, underlined sigla). Key K3k, trained on declared pairs in the same chancery hand (3594,149↔148, 158↔157, 160↔159, 151↔150 pp. 1-2, 3595,308↔309), frozen, then tested on 3594,151 image 3 ↔ 150 never seen: 0.888 of characters / 0.812 of words (normalised spelling; 200 controls p99 0.313 / 0.161), validated. Reading of 312: 884 words, about 87-88 % read by sense (61 unresolved, 57 restored, 8 probable), below the 95 % rule; what remains is the nomenclator (44 codes), not the signs. Subject: the negotiation with Genoa (passes, exchange of prisoners, galleys), answering Siruela's letters of 4 and 20 Oct 1638. Reported by Brice Dudout from his own look at the images; not yet checked here.
why: A royal despatch to Genoa entirely in cipher, probably never deciphered in print; the key family is known (genes1638), so a full reading looks within reach.
score_note: Images viewed (all 4) and fully transcribed by Brice Dudout's agents; key validated, reading about 87-88 %, not yet at 95 %.
verify: The nomenclator codes (44 unresolved): the sent original or a plain copy in Genoa, or other royal despatches to Siruela in the same hand.

title: Riverbank Laboratories 'Mexican codes' and unsorted cryptographic papers (the surviving Riverbank Department of Ciphers files)
correspondents: Mexican government / agents (intercepted) -> Riverbank Department of Ciphers (W. F. and E. S. Friedman) for the State, War, Navy and Justice Departments
shelfmark: New York Public Library, Manuscripts and Archives Division, MssCol 176 (Bacon cipher collection), box 15 'Riverbank Labs -- student exercises and lessons, Mexican codes' and box 16 'Riverbank Labs -- unsorted material concerning cryptography'
folio_note: Box-level description only (1982 accession sheet, 33 boxes). Not digitised (NYPL Digital Collections shows 10 Baconian items only). Contents unknown: could be worksheets, intercept copies or training exercises built from them.
status: Friedman's own accounts (NSA Friedman papers, folders 433/513) say Riverbank worked codes and ciphers forwarded by State, War, Navy and Justice in 1916-20; a 1917 Army note quoted in a web search summary says the main work was Mexican messages (source PDF not opened). Friedman wrote in 1948 that the Riverbank cipher records were thought destroyed after Fabyan's death (Cora Tyzzer letter, NSA A69876) and that the LoC Fabyan collection held none of them; the NYPL boxes came via Fabyan's widow to George Curtis (gift 1960), so these two boxes may be the only survivors. MI-8 broke several Mexican government codes in 1917-19 (repo: research/nara_triage_c/e), so many messages will be read; whether any are unread is unknown. Schmeh (2018) saw three boxes, not these. NSA historians (Dave Hatch and a colleague, a November visit, year not given) went through all nine Riverbank boxes and found them 'very duplicative and mixed': page proofs of Riverbank publications, student folders and exercises on graph paper, a few Parker Hitt letters; no cipher intercepts are mentioned (NSA blog 'A great TDY', Doc ID 6919113, released 30 Mar 2026).
why: The only known surviving working files of the first US government cryptanalytic unit (Riverbank 1917-18); any message they hold unread is WWI German-Mexican traffic.
score_note: Scored from the archive description during the Oct 2026 Riverbank sweep (research/chi_riverbank/); not viewed
verify: Request boxes 15 and 16 of MssCol 176 (NYPL Brooke Russell Astor Reading Room, appointment); list each cipher text and whether a solution sheet is with it; compare with the MID 10020 Riverbank monthly 'undeciphered messages' reports (catalogue 674).
